content:
The tea shop after closing had a different kind of silence.

During the day, every sound belonged to someone: cups touching saucers, chairs moving across the floor, customers laughing, the kettle announcing that it had been ignored. At night, the quiet belonged to the wood, the walls, the jasmine plant, and the two of us.

Iroh began locking the door earlier.

“You are becoming suspicious,” I said.

“I am becoming efficient.”

“You closed thirty minutes early.”

“The chairs were tired.”

“The chairs have no feelings.”

“You have met very few chairs.”

I stood behind the counter, sorting tea leaves into small tins. Iroh moved through the shop with a candle in one hand. The light caught the silver in his hair.

“Are you going to help?” I asked.

“I am supervising.”

“You are watching me.”

“That is part of supervision.”

“You have been watching me for five minutes.”

“A thorough supervisor is a good supervisor.”

I put the tin down. “Come here.”

Iroh's eyebrows lifted. “That sounded like an order.”

“You can refuse.”

“I could.”

“Are you going to?”

“No.”

He crossed the room. I met him beside the counter. His hands settled at my waist.

“Still comfortable?” he asked.

“You are becoming predictable.”

“I am becoming careful.”

“You can be both.”

He kissed me.

The kiss was slow, but the shop held the heat of it. Iroh pressed close enough that I felt the strength of him through his clothes. I touched his shoulders, then the back of his neck. He made a quiet sound against my mouth.

“That was not very scholarly,” I murmured.

“I have studied many subjects.”

“Was kissing one of them?”

“I am conducting research.”

“The experiment is going well.”

“I am pleased.”

He kissed the corner of my mouth, then my cheek. His fingers traced the line of my back, pausing whenever my breath changed.

The candle flame bent in the draft. Outside, a cart rolled past, its driver singing under his breath.

“We should go upstairs,” Iroh said.

“Why?”

“Because the shop has windows.”

“You are concerned about being seen?”

“I am concerned about giving the neighborhood an unnecessarily interesting morning.”

I laughed. He kissed me again, longer this time.

“You know,” I said, “you could just say you want privacy.”

“I want privacy.”

“Good.”

He took my hand. We locked the back door together. The stairs creaked beneath me.

Upstairs, the room smelled of jasmine and rain. The balcony doors were open. Iroh closed them, then turned to me.

“We should talk,” he said.

“That sounds ominous.”

“It is about the future.”

“The future is always ominous when someone says it like that.”

He took off his outer coat and draped it over the chair.

“You may not wish to remain above the shop forever,” he said. “You may want a place entirely your own.”

“I know.”

“You may decide the work is not what you want.”

“I know.”

“You may decide you do not want me.”

“I know.”

He looked at me. “I am telling you because I do not want tonight to become a promise you feel required to keep.”

The tenderness of it made my chest ache.

“I want tonight,” I said.

“That is enough.”

“And I want tomorrow.”

“That is also enough.”

“And I want to see what happens after tomorrow.”

Iroh stepped closer. “Then we will see it.”

I reached for him. “Can I kiss you?”

His smile was warm. “You may.”

The kiss carried all the conversations I had not finished. His hands were careful, but no longer hesitant. I knew the questions he would ask. He knew the ways I answered.

When the heat between us grew, he paused.

“Still comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Do you wish to stop?”

“No.”

“Then we may continue.”

The lamp went out.

The rest of the evening remained ours: quiet, affectionate, and sheltered from the city beyond the balcony.

In the morning, I found Iroh asleep beside me, one hand open on the blanket between us. I placed my hand in it.

His fingers closed around mine without waking.

The tea shop below would open soon.

For a little longer, I let the world wait.

When I woke, Iroh was already watching the dawn through the balcony doors.

“You are awake,” he said.

“You are staring.”

“I am observing.”

“That is what you call staring.”

“It is a more respectable word.”

I sat up. His outer robe was draped over the chair. The room smelled of jasmine and rain.

“Did you sleep?” I asked.

“Eventually.”

“You are using my answer.”

“It is a useful one.”

He brought me tea in the cup with my name. I accepted it.

“The shop opens in an hour,” I said.

“Then we should not be here.”

“You are the owner.”

“A poor excuse for lateness.”

“You have been late before.”

“I was younger.”

“You are using age again.”

“It remains effective.”

I drank. The tea was perfect.

“I want to ask about work,” I said.

Iroh sat at the edge of the bed. “Ask.”

“Do you still want me as an employee?”

“Yes.”

“Even if we are together?”

“Yes.”

“What if one of us has a bad day?”

“We do not punish the other with silence.”

“What if we argue?”

“We step away from the customers. We do not use wages or housing as weapons.”

“What if we break up?”

The question changed the room.

Iroh looked at me for a long moment. “Then we make a plan that protects your home and your work. You will not lose the room because a relationship ended.”

My eyes burned.

“You mean that?”

“Yes.”

“Even if you are hurt?”

“Especially then.”

The answer was not romantic in the way songs were romantic. It was better. It gave love a structure strong enough to hold pain without turning it into punishment.

I reached for him. He took my hand.

“I do not plan to break up with you,” he said.

“I know.”

“But a plan should include difficult possibilities.”

“You are very responsible.”

“It is a burden.”

“You can set it down sometimes.”

“I am trying.”

I kissed him. He smiled against my mouth.

The shop bell rang downstairs.

“We are late,” I said.

“The customers may survive.”

“The kettle will not.”

“The kettle is immortal.”

We dressed together, bumping shoulders in the narrow room. Iroh tied his sash while I searched for the key to the shop.

“It is in your pocket,” he said.

“How do you know?”

“I am observing.”

I found it in his pocket instead.

“You stole my key.”

“I was keeping it safe.”

“From what?”

“Your forgetfulness.”

I took it back and kissed him again.

Downstairs, the first customer pretended not to notice that my hair was untidy and Iroh's robe was tied incorrectly.

The shop opened.

The day began.

That night, I made a new rule: one evening each week belonged to neither the shop nor the road. It belonged to me.

Iroh agreed.

Then he asked whether tea counted as work.

I told him it depended on whether he was making it for customers or for me.

He smiled. “Then I know what to brew.”

The first evening belonging only to me began with a walk to the river. Iroh brought no notebook, no letters, and no map. I carried a small basket of food.

“You have planned,” he said.

“I have planned not to plan.”

“An advanced discipline.”

I sat beneath a tree. The river reflected the lanterns from the bridge. Iroh poured tea from a flask.

“Is this shop tea?” I asked.

“It is personal tea.”

“What is the difference?”

“The shop tea is measured. The personal tea is made by feeling.”

I tasted it. It was softer than his usual blend, with honey and citrus.

“It is good,” I said.

“You sound surprised.”

“You made it by feeling.”

“My feelings are refined.”

“Your feelings are dramatic.”

“Refined drama.”

I leaned against his shoulder.

“What do you want to do when there is nothing to fix?” I asked.

Iroh thought. “Sit with you.”

“That is all?”

“Some days, yes.”

“You could play pai sho.”

“You would lose.”

“I could throw a tile.”

“A powerful strategy.”

I laughed. The evening passed without a crisis. It felt like a rare kind of magic.

When I returned to the shop, Iroh opened the door and held it for me.

“You first,” he said.

“You are becoming polite.”

“I am becoming romantic.”

“You have always been romantic.”

“I have been hiding it beneath tea.”

“Poorly.”

He kissed me in the doorway.

The kiss lasted until the river lanterns blurred behind my closed eyes.

When I finally separated, Iroh kept his forehead against mine and asked whether tomorrow could belong to the shop again.

“Only if tonight belongs to us,” I said.

“It does.”

I walked home beneath the lanterns with my hands joined.

The night was quiet around me.

The quiet followed me to the shop door and waited while Iroh found the key.

The night was quiet around me.
